young.html: Willa Cather grew up on the prairies of Nebraska, where pioneer families had built farms and towns along the new railroads. She wrote novels about those pioneers and the land.

In A Lost Lady, a boy named Niel lives in a little railroad town called Sweet Water. On a hill outside town is the house of Captain Forrester, a grand old man who helped build the railroads, and his lively, charming wife. The boys of the town love to play in the Forresters' meadow. As Niel grows up, he sees the Captain grow old and lose his money, and he sees the bold pioneer days give way to a time of people who care only about getting rich.

young.html: Then and now. Ask a grandparent or older neighbor what your town was like when they were young. What was there that is gone now? What is new? Draw two pictures of the same street, "then" and "now."

full.html: Willa Cather (1873–1947) moved as a child from Virginia to Red Cloud, Nebraska, a town on the Burlington railroad. She became a magazine editor in New York and then a novelist, writing of the prairie in O Pioneers! and My Ántonia. Her novel One of Ours won the Pulitzer Prize in 1923, the year A Lost Lady appeared. She based Mrs. Forrester partly on a woman she had known in Red Cloud. The book begins:

full.text: Thirty or forty years ago, in one of those grey towns along the Burlington railroad, there was a house well known from Omaha to Denver for its hospitality and for a certain charm of atmosphere.
full.author: Cather
full.work: A Lost Lady, Part I, chapter I
full.note: The Gutenberg text was made from a later printing of Knopf's edition.

full.html: Captain Daniel Forrester built railroads across the West. He loves his marsh and meadow as they are:

full.text: Any one but Captain Forrester would have drained the bottom land and made it into highly productive fields.
full.author: Cather
full.work: A Lost Lady, Part I, chapter I

full.html: We see the Forresters mostly through Niel Herbert, who as a boy worships the Captain's gracious wife, Marian. One summer day a mean-spirited older boy, Ivy Peters, hurts a woodpecker for fun, and Niel, trying to rescue it, falls from a tree and is cared for in the Forresters' house. As Niel grows up, a bank in Denver fails, and the Captain gives up his fortune to repay its small depositors rather than let them lose their savings. He suffers strokes and declines. Niel is disillusioned to learn that Mrs. Forrester is not the perfect lady he imagined, and that after the Captain's death she turns for help to Ivy Peters, now a sharp lawyer who drains the Captain's marsh for profit. Years later Niel hears that she married again in South America and was well cared for to the end.

full.html: The "lost lady" is both Mrs. Forrester and an age. The pioneers, Cather writes, were dreamers and builders; the generation after them were shrewd men who drained the marshes and cut up the land for gain.
Cather tells the story in short, clear scenes and leaves much unsaid. She called this the "novel démeublé," the unfurnished novel: take out the clutter, and let the reader feel what is left out.
Reading Niel as always right. He judges Mrs. Forrester harshly by an ideal she never claimed; Cather lets us see her love of life, and her courage, more fairly than he does.

items: Fitzgerald's Great Gatsby, two years later and later on this ladder, also has a young narrator who watches and judges a glamorous figure; Fitzgerald wrote to Cather that he feared he had echoed her.
Flaubert's Madame Bovary and Tolstoy wrote of women trapped by marriage and longing; Cather is gentler with her heroine.
Tocqueville's Democracy in America, earlier on this ladder, described the restless American drive to get ahead that the book's Ivy Peters stands for.
Frederick Jackson Turner's idea of the closing frontier (1893) is the history behind the story.
Is it fair to judge people by the ideal picture we have of them?
What is lost when wild land is "improved" for profit, and what is gained?
Why does the Captain choose to repay the depositors? What does it cost him?
What do the pioneers and the generation after them each value?

questions: The Captain gave up his fortune to keep a promise to ordinary people. What do you think of that?
Why did Niel feel let down by Mrs. Forrester?
Ivy Peters hurt a bird for fun as a boy. What does that tell us about the man he became?
What does your town keep from its past? What has it lost?
Can someone be both admirable and flawed?
care: One early scene shows a boy's cruelty to a bird, and the book mentions an adult secret romance without detail.
